title: Lists
intro: A **list** holds several values in order, inside square brackets: `["bread", "eggs", "milk"]`. Lists can grow and shrink, and each item has a position (index) starting at **0**.

questions.prompt: Use an index in square brackets to read one item. Negative indexes count from the end, so `-1` is the last item.
questions.explanation: `len()` tells you how many items a list has.

questions.prompt: Create a list called `primes` containing the numbers `2, 3, 5, 7` in that order.

tests.name: is list
tests.code: assert isinstance(primes, list), 'primes should be a list — use square brackets.'

tests.name: values
tests.code: assert primes == [2, 3, 5, 7], 'primes should contain 2, 3, 5, 7 in that order.'

questions.explanation: Order matters in a list: `[2, 3]` and `[3, 2]` are different lists.

questions.hint: Indexes start at 0: red is 0, green is 1…

questions.prompt: `queue` holds people waiting. Store the **last** person in a variable called `last` using a negative index.

tests.name: last
tests.code: assert last == 'Dev', 'last should be the final item in queue.'

questions.hint: `queue[-1]` is the last item, whatever the list's length.
questions.explanation: Negative indexes keep working when the list grows.

questions.prompt: Add `"oats"` to the **end** of `pantry`, then change the first item from `"rice"` to `"pasta"`.
questions.hint: `list.append(x)` adds to the end. Assign to an index to replace an item: `pantry[0] = ...`.
questions.explanation: Lists are mutable: you change them in place rather than making a new one.

questions.hint: With 3 items the valid indexes are 0, 1 and 2.
questions.explanation: Reading past the end raises `IndexError: list index out of range`.

questions.prompt: This should remove `"spam"` from `inbox`, but it crashes. Fix it so `"spam"` is removed.
questions.hint: `remove()` takes the **value** to delete, not its position. (`pop(1)` would remove by position.)
questions.explanation: Use `remove(value)` when you know the value and `pop(index)` when you know the position.

questions.prompt: Loop over `temps` and print each temperature on its own line followed by `°C` — for example `21°C`.
questions.hint: `for t in temps:` then an indented `print(f"{t}°C")`.
questions.explanation: A `for` loop visits each item in order; the f-string glues the unit on.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so `count` holds the number of items in `guests`.

tests.name: count
tests.code: assert count == 5, 'count should be the length of guests.'

questions.hint: One built-in function returns the length of a list.
questions.explanation: `len()` works on lists, strings, tuples, dictionaries and sets.

questions.prompt: Create `top_three` holding the first three items of `scores` using a slice.

tests.name: slice
tests.code: assert top_three == [98, 91, 87], 'top_three should be the first three scores.'
tests.message: Use a slice for the first three.

tests.name: original untouched
tests.code: assert scores == [98, 91, 87, 76, 70], 'Do not change scores itself.'

questions.hint: `list[start:stop]` — leave start empty to begin at 0; stop is not included.
questions.explanation: Slicing makes a new list and leaves the original alone.
